prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A college student who survived a boat sinking with four others said Monday that a safety officer who died on their boat was a hero for staying behind and pushing him out. Texas A&M student Steven Guy, left, and instructor Steve Conway talk about their boat capsizing. Steven Guy, a Texas A&M University sailor, said Roger Stone saved him and another sailor by helping them to safety. "He is my hero," Guy said. "He saved me. If it wasn't for him, I would not be here." The group never saw Stone after he pushed the two men out of a hatch in the boat, the mariners said. Stone, the boat's second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon. The two men said they spent a day in open water after their vessel sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The survivors -- four university students and a safety officer -- told the Coast Guard they were forced off their sailboat after it took on water and capsized early Saturday. The five survivors were found and airlifted to land around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Coast Guard said. The group had to get out of the rapidly sinking sailboat so quickly, they could get only four safety vests for five people, safety officer Steve Conway said Monday. They had to huddle in the water to keep each other afloat, he said.  Watch the rescue and see Conway describe the ordeal » . "With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely," he said. "These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live." R. Bowen Loftin, CEO  and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, expressed condolences to the Stone family in a letter posted along with status updates on the school's Web site. "We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival," Loftin said on the site. "We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word." Conway said that as the group huddled in the water, they saw rescue jets go by three times before they were spotted. "It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves," he said. Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who was flying the aircraft that rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight helped save them. While conducting search patterns, Coast Guard members spotted the light through their night vision goggles, Rivera said. It was being held by one of the men. He said that because the Coast Guard was searching such a vast area, the flashlight was "instrumental" in the rescue. "It's your proverbial needle in a haystack," Rivera told KHOU. During the 26-hour wait, the group was nibbled by curious reed fish and circled by a fish with triangular fin that extended from the water like a shark's fin. "They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes," Conway said. "You don't know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks." The group's sailboat, named the Cynthia Woods, was one of about two dozen boats heading from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, for the annual Veracruz Regatta race, which began Friday.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — A college student who survived a boat sinking with four others said Monday that a safety officer who died aboard the vessel was a hero for staying behind and pushing him to safety.

Texas A&M student Steven Guy, left, and instructor Steve Conway discuss the capsizing of their boat.

Guy, a sailor at Texas A&M University, said Roger Stone saved him and another sailor by helping them escape.

“He is my hero,” Guy said. “He saved me. If it wasn’t for him, I would not be here.”

The mariners said they never saw Stone again after he pushed the two men through a hatch. Stone, the boat’s second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon.

The two men said they spent a day in open water after their vessel sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The survivors—four university students and a safety officer—told the Coast Guard they were forced to abandon their sailboat after it took on water and capsized early Saturday.

The five survivors were found and airlifted to land at around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Coast Guard said.

Safety officer Steve Conway said Monday that the group had to escape the rapidly sinking sailboat so quickly that they were able to retrieve only four life jackets for five people. They huddled together in the water to keep one another afloat, he said.

Watch the rescue and hear Conway describe the ordeal »

“With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely,” Conway said. “These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live.”

R. Bowen Loftin, CEO and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, expressed condolences to Stone’s family in a letter posted alongside status updates on the school’s website.

“We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival,” Loftin wrote. “We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word.”

Conway said that while the group huddled in the water, they watched rescue aircraft pass overhead three times before they were spotted.

“It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves,” he said.

Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who was aboard the aircraft that rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight helped save them. While conducting search patterns, Coast Guard personnel spotted the light through their night-vision goggles, Rivera said. One of the men was holding it.

Because the Coast Guard was searching such a vast area, Rivera said, the flashlight was “instrumental” in the rescue.

“It’s your proverbial needle in a haystack,” Rivera told KHOU.

During the 26-hour wait, the group was nibbled by curious reed fish and circled by a fish whose triangular fin protruded from the water like a shark’s fin.

“They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes,” Conway said. “You don’t know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks.”

The group’s sailboat, the *Cynthia Woods*, was one of about two dozen vessels traveling from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, for the annual Veracruz Regatta, which began Friday.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Monday, a college student who survived a sailboat sinking along with four other people praised the safety officer who died after remaining aboard long enough to push him to safety.

Texas A&M student and sailor Steven Guy, pictured on the left with instructor Steve Conway as they discussed the capsizing, said Roger Stone helped him and another sailor escape.

Guy called Stone his hero, saying Stone saved his life and that he would not be alive without him.

The sailors said they never saw Stone again after he pushed both men through a hatch. Stone, who served as the vessel’s second safety officer, was recovered dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon.

Guy and Conway said they remained in the open waters of the Gulf of Mexico for about a day after the boat went down. According to the five survivors—four Texas A&M students and one safety officer—the sailboat began taking on water and overturned early Saturday, forcing them to abandon it.

The Coast Guard located the group at approximately 2 a.m. Sunday and flew them back to shore.

Conway said Monday that the vessel sank so rapidly that they escaped with only four life jackets for the five people. To remain afloat, the survivors stayed clustered together in the water.

Because one person lacked a flotation vest, Conway said, the others had to monitor that individual carefully. He commended the students for enduring the ordeal, saying they showed an intense determination to survive.

In a letter published with updates on the university’s website, R. Bowen Loftin, CEO and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, offered condolences to Stone’s family. Loftin wrote that the family might find some comfort in knowing that all five survivors believed Stone’s courageous actions were crucial to keeping them alive. He added that Stone had died a hero in the truest, traditional meaning of the term.

While the group waited together in the water, Conway said, rescue aircraft passed overhead three times before anyone noticed them. He described how disheartening it was to see a plane fly over and then depart.

Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, the pilot of the aircraft involved in the rescue, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight played a key role in finding the survivors. During the search, Coast Guard personnel saw the beam—held by one of the men—through night-vision goggles.

Rivera said the light was essential because rescuers were covering an enormous search zone. He compared locating the group to finding the proverbial needle in a haystack.

During their 26 hours in the water, curious reed fish bumped into the survivors and nibbled at their clothing. They were also circled by a fish whose triangular fin protruded above the surface like that of a shark.

Conway said they could not tell how large or hungry the animal might be, and he remained conscious of the potential danger posed by sharks.

The sailboat, called the *Cynthia Woods*, was among roughly two dozen vessels traveling from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, as part of the annual Veracruz Regatta, which started Friday.

outputs.L4:
A Texas A&M University sailboat capsized in the Gulf of Mexico, abruptly trapping its six crew members inside the overturned vessel. With water rushing into the cabin, the sailors had only moments to find an escape route. Five eventually reached the surface, but safety officer Roger Stone remained below long enough to help two of the others squeeze through a narrow hatch. His decision cost him the chance to escape, and he died inside the boat.

Once in the open water, the survivors faced another ordeal. They had escaped so quickly that they were left with only four life jackets for five people. For roughly a day, they stayed together in the Gulf, sharing the flotation devices and struggling against fatigue, exposure, and uncertainty. With no immediate way to summon help, they relied on one another while waiting and hoping that rescuers would locate them.

The Coast Guard ultimately found the group and brought all five survivors to safety. In recounting the disaster, they emphasized that their rescue would not have been possible without Stone’s actions. Rather than saving himself, he stayed behind in the flooding cabin and pushed two trapped sailors through the hatch, giving them the opportunity to join the others at the surface.

Stone’s sacrifice became the defining act of the tragedy. Although the loss devastated his family, friends, and the Texas A&M sailing community, the survivors remembered him as a hero whose courage and selflessness allowed five others to come home.
